messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Thompson is a 67-year-old married man who has been working as a hotel manager for over three decades. His experience with a mugging several months ago has significantly altered his daily life and has brought him to seek psychological help today. The traumatic event occurred during one of his routine late-night shifts at the hotel. A masked individual, acting suspiciously, approached Mr. Thompson from behind, overpowering him and stealing his wallet and phone. The incident was sudden, with the mugging taking place in a dimly lit area near the back entrance of the building. The smell of alcohol emanating from the assailant is vividly etched into his memory. Since that night, Mr. Thompson has been hyperalert to any potential threats around him, particularly when people act suspiciously or make loud noises. His hypervigilance has become a constant presence in his life; he finds himself on edge even inside his own home. The sense of mistrust and the feeling that the world is dangerous have reinforced this heightened state of alertness. Mr. Thompson’s negative appraisals, particularly his belief that people can’t be trusted and that he feels permanently humiliated by what happened, contribute to his heightened threat perception. He has come to believe that others cannot be relied upon for safety or support, which makes him even more vigilant in detecting potential threats. For example, during a recent staff meeting at the hotel, an employee’s casual comment about someone acting suspiciously triggered Mr. Thompson's alarm bells. The incident led him to react sharply and withdraw from further interaction with his colleagues, fearing another attack. Even the smell of alcohol now triggers intense anxiety for Mr. Thompson. During one evening when he was out running errands near a bar, the strong scent of liquor brought back memories of the mugging in such vivid detail that he felt physically shaken and had to leave the area quickly. This experience has made him extremely wary of environments where there is even a hint of alcohol. Mr. Thompson’s hypervigilance has also affected his home life. He feels on guard even inside his own house, constantly checking locks and monitoring any unusual sounds or movements around him. His heightened state of alertness has led to sleep disturbances, making it difficult for him to rest peacefully at night. This constant anxiety has strained his relationship with his wife, who finds herself increasingly concerned about his well-being. Despite the significant impact on his daily life, Mr. Thompson’s reluctance to trust others and his feeling of permanent humiliation have made it challenging for him to seek help until now. His belief that he cannot fully rely on anyone for support has been a barrier in opening up about his struggles. However, the continuous intrusion of triggers and the constant sense of threat have become too overwhelming, pushing him to finally reach out for psychological assistance. What frightens Mr. Thompson most is the possibility of another attack and the lasting damage it might cause to his mental health and relationships. He hopes that with support, he can regain a sense of safety and trust in the world around him. His journey toward healing begins today, as he takes the first step towards addressing the fears and anxieties that have been controlling his life since the mugging.
